title: 1 Samuel 25:1–13
context: Chapter 25 opens with the death of Samuel, mourned by all Israel and buried at Ramah, a brief notice that marks the passing of the prophet who anointed both Saul and David. David, still a fugitive from Saul, moves into the wilderness; the Hebrew text says Paran, while some Greek manuscripts read Maon, which fits the setting of the next verse. There he asks Nabal, a wealthy and surly man of Maon with flocks at Carmel, for provisions in return for the protection his men had given Nabal’s shepherds. Nabal answers with insult, and David straps on his sword with four hundred men, intent on revenge. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this as shared ground: the story contrasts folly and wisdom, and shows the anointed king-in-waiting on the edge of a grave sin.

verses.text: Samuel died; and all Israel gathered themselves together and mourned for him, and buried him at his house at Ramah. Then David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the brief but weighty notice that Samuel died and all Israel mourned him at Ramah (compare 1 Samuel 28:3). The prophet who anointed Saul and David passes from the story, leaving David to walk by faith without him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the death of Samuel as marking a transition in God’s dealings with Israel, while his purposes for David continue. The Hebrew reads Paran where some Greek manuscripts read Maon, and readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact location with caution.

verses.text: There was a man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel; and the man was very great. He had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Nabal introduced as a very great man with large flocks, his wealth evident from the numbers given. Prosperity sets the stage for a test of generosity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Maon and Carmel here are towns of Judah (compare Joshua 15:55), generally distinguished from Mount Carmel in the north. Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the contrast between Nabal’s abundance and his stinginess.

verses.text: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail. This woman was intelligent and had a beautiful face; but the man was surly and evil in his doings. He was of the house of Caleb.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sharp contrast between Abigail, intelligent and beautiful, and Nabal, surly and evil in his doings. Character, not wealth, will decide the outcome of the story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nabal is of the house of Caleb, a family with an honorable heritage (compare Joshua 14:13) that he does not live up to. Readers in both traditions commonly see the narrator inviting moral evaluation from the start.

verses.text: David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David hears of the sheep shearing, an occasion David’s men will call a good day (25:8). The festive moment offers Nabal a natural opportunity to show kindness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shearing season as the setting for a request that tests Nabal’s heart. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a simple narrative step toward the request that follows.

verses.text: David sent ten young men; and David said to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David sending ten young men to greet Nabal in his name, a courteous and formal approach. The request begins with honor, not demand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the respectful greeting as fitting the customs of the time. Readers in both traditions commonly note that David’s initial approach is gracious.

verses.text: Tell him, ‘Long life to you! Peace be to you! Peace be to your house! Peace be to all that you have!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the repeated blessing of peace on Nabal, his house and all he has. David’s message opens with goodwill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the greeting as expressing a sincere wish for Nabal’s welfare. Both traditions commonly read the warm language as setting up the harshness of Nabal’s reply.

verses.text: Now I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds have now been with us, and we didn’t harm them. Nothing was missing from them all the time they were in Carmel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David reminding Nabal that his shepherds were protected and lost nothing while near David’s men. Kindness has already been shown and can be confirmed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal to past protection as a reasonable basis for asking a gift in return. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Nabal’s own servants later confirm this account (25:15–16).

verses.text: Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let the young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a good day. Please give whatever comes to your hand to your servants and to your son David.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note David’s humble request for whatever Nabal can spare, calling himself Nabal’s son. The tone is respectful and modest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the request as fitting what his men call a good day, when sharing would be natural. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that David asks rather than seizes.

verses.text: When David’s young men came, they spoke to Nabal all those words in the name of David, and waited.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David’s young men faithfully delivering the message and waiting for a reply. They act with restraint and courtesy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the waiting as giving Nabal every opportunity to respond well. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as building suspense before Nabal’s answer.

verses.text: Nabal answered David’s servants and said, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants who break away from their masters these days.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Nabal’s contemptuous questions about who David is, likening him to runaway servants. His words insult David publicly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Nabal belittles the one God has chosen to be king (compare 1 Samuel 16:13). Both traditions commonly read the reply as revealing a proud and ungrateful heart.

verses.text: Shall I then take my bread, my water, and my meat that I have killed for my shearers, and give it to men who I don’t know where they come from?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Nabal’s repeated use of my, my bread, my water and my meat, showing a self-centered view of his possessions. He forgets that what he has is from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Nabal’s refusal as a failure of gratitude and neighborliness. Readers in both traditions commonly connect his attitude with the folly his name suggests, which 25:25 itself explains (Nabal means foolish).

verses.text: So David’s young men turned on their way and went back, and came and told him all these words.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the young men returning and reporting Nabal’s words exactly. The insult is now in David’s hands to answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as the turning point where David must choose his response. Both traditions commonly read it as setting up the danger of David acting in anger.

verses.text: David said to his men, “Every man put on his sword!” Every man put on his sword. David also put on his sword. About four hundred men followed David, and two hundred stayed by the baggage.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David’s quick command for every man to put on his sword, a sign of rising anger. Even a man after God’s heart can be tempted toward rash vengeance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David on the verge of serious sin, showing that God’s chosen servants still need restraining grace. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober warning about responding to insult with violence.
